name: Imaging Centers
description: Medical imaging helps clinicians examine internal structures and investigate disease or injury. Research from Iran shows why the availability of scanners must be considered alongside their geographic distribution and the clinical services they support.

seo.title: Imaging Centers in Iran: Technology and Access | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand CT and MRI services in Iran, the history of scanner diffusion, and the limits of equipment counts as measures of healthcare access.

content.heading: Different technologies answer different questions
content.content:
An imaging service produces pictures that help clinicians investigate structures inside the body. Two important technologies are computed tomography, usually called CT, and magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI. Understanding their differences makes it easier to interpret discussions of equipment investment in Iran: counting machines together can obscure the different services they provide. [s1][s2]

CT uses a rotating X-ray source and computer processing to construct cross-sectional images. These images can also be assembled into three-dimensional views. Its applications include investigating injuries, internal bleeding, tumors, and abnormalities in different organs. Because CT uses X-rays, radiation exposure forms part of its clinical risk–benefit assessment. A detailed image is useful when it answers an appropriate clinical question; image production alone does not establish a diagnosis. [s1]

MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses to generate images. It is particularly useful for examining soft tissues, including the brain, spinal cord, muscles, and ligaments. It does not use the ionizing X-rays employed by CT. This distinction does not make every MRI examination suitable for every person: magnetic fields, implanted devices, and other safety considerations require appropriate screening. These are general technological principles, rather than evidence about the performance of any particular Iranian center. [s2]

content.heading: How advanced imaging spread
content.content: An early study of MRI diffusion in Iran used Ministry of Health equipment information and questionnaires to medical universities. It traced the acquisition of the first MRI unit to 1990 and described faster adoption later in the decade, with a growing private-sector contribution. The provincial distribution did not simply follow population size. The authors therefore emphasized health technology assessment: evaluating the value and appropriate use of equipment when deciding where it should be introduced. This is historical evidence about diffusion, rather than a current inventory of centers. [s3]

content.heading: More scanners can coexist with unequal access
content.content:
Research in Lorestan, a province in western Iran, compared public-hospital CT and MRI distribution in 2014 and 2023. Equipment expanded, but the authors found greater inequality in its distribution across the study locations. Their discussion connects equipment allocation with the concentration of hospitals, specialists, and expected demand in larger cities. [s4]

The study has important boundaries. It did not establish how additional equipment changed clinical outcomes, and it cannot represent every province or private imaging center. Scanner distribution also cannot establish waiting times, affordability, machine uptime, or the availability of expert interpretation. The practical conclusion is that an imaging network should be understood through both technical capacity and access to a functioning clinical service. [s4]

name: Home Care
description: Home care brings professional health services into the household, including support after hospital discharge and care for people with continuing needs. Iranian qualitative research highlights the importance of family relationships, trained personnel, financing, and oversight in making these services dependable.

seo.title: Home Care in Iran: Nursing, Families and Service Quality | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore professional home care in Iran through research on nursing practice, family expectations, service costs, training, and quality oversight.

content.heading: Care enters a different working environment
content.content:
Home care moves professional services into the place where a person lives. Iranian nursing research describes work extending from support after hospital discharge to care for older people and people with disabilities or continuing health needs. The household becomes a care setting, bringing clinical work into close contact with family routines and relationships. [s1]

This setting changes the conditions of practice. Nurses interviewed in Tehran and Khorasan described difficult care situations, economic pressures, professional barriers, social difficulties, and bureaucratic tensions. Their accounts show why a home visit involves more than transporting a hospital task to another address: equipment, professional support, interpersonal boundaries, and the safety of the visiting worker all shape delivery. The findings document participants’ experiences; they do not measure how often each problem occurs across Iran. [s1]

content.heading: Families and the health system both shape provision
content.content:
A qualitative study conducted in Iran in 2015 examined home care through interviews with policymakers, clinicians, patients, and family members. It identified a treatment-oriented health system, cultural expectations, and inadequate infrastructure as important barriers. Including patients and relatives matters because professional service design and household expectations may differ. [s2]

The study’s findings also help explain why home care cannot be understood solely as a private arrangement between a nurse and a family. Its place within the wider health system affects how services are organized and supported. The researchers argued for clearer integration, attention to cultural conditions, and suitable infrastructure. These are findings and recommendations from that research period, rather than a description of current legal entitlements or insurance coverage. [s2]

content.heading: Quality depends on the service around the visit
content.content:
Research conducted in Isfahan in 2022 and published in 2024 distinguished infrastructure problems from problems in the delivery process. Participants discussed public acceptance, service economics, staffing, policymaking, quality improvement, and the facilities needed to provide care. The authors recommended stronger workforce preparation, monitoring, accreditation, and attention to insurance financing. These recommendations should not be read as proof that a particular funding or accreditation arrangement has since been implemented. [s3]

The Isfahan study explicitly cautions against generalizing qualitative findings to other communities. Together, these studies provide a useful picture of recurring concerns while leaving room for differences between cities, agencies, and households. They do not establish national patient outcomes or demonstrate that home care consistently reduces expenditure. The central issue is continuity: a visit becomes more valuable when competent staff, appropriate resources, and dependable organizational support sustain the care around it. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Health Technology
description: This branch explores the digital systems used to record, coordinate, and deliver healthcare in Iran. Research on electronic records and telemedicine shows both their practical potential and the organizational, infrastructure, and governance conditions needed for effective use.

seo.title: Health Technology in Iran: Records, Systems and Telemedicine | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An evidence-based introduction to Iran’s digital health systems, including SEPAS, SIB, hospital information exchange, and barriers to telemedicine.

content.heading: From recording an encounter to supporting care
content.content:
Within this branch, health technology means the digital systems that support healthcare information and communication. A useful starting distinction is between recording an encounter, exchanging information between organizations, and making that information useful during care. Iranian research shows that these are related achievements, each requiring more than the installation of software. [s1][s2]

A hospital information system manages information generated within a hospital. An electronic health record has a broader ambition: maintaining information across encounters and potentially across organizations. SEPAS, Iran’s national electronic health record initiative, receives information from hospital systems through infrastructure hosted at medical universities. The transferred material described in research includes demographic details, diagnoses, procedures, test results, and billing information. This architecture establishes a route for information exchange; it does not establish that every clinician can use a complete longitudinal record at every consultation. [s1]

content.heading: Primary care has its own information needs
content.content:
SIB, Iran’s Integrated Electronic Health System, supports primary-care documentation. Its functions described in research include registering people and services, recording vaccination and pregnancy care, identifying risk factors, and supporting screening and reporting. These tasks concern continuing care for a covered population, giving the system a different working context from a hospital admission record. [s2]

A qualitative study in health centers in Ahvaz, Shoushtar, and Omidiyeh, in Khuzestan province, found both benefits and difficulties. Participants described faster information retrieval, less paperwork, and improved reporting, alongside training problems, internet interruptions, costs, and additional documentation workload. Concerns also included confidentiality and whether recorded services accurately represented care delivered. These findings explain why data quality and staff experience belong in any assessment of digital health. They are local accounts, rather than national estimates of satisfaction or service improvement. [s2]

content.heading: National infrastructure needs evaluation in practice
content.content: A study of SEPAS users conducted in 2021 and published in 2023 examined system success through a structured information-systems evaluation model. Its authors identified stability problems and limited benefits for patient-centered service delivery. The research focused on personnel working with information transfer and management in selected teaching hospitals. Their experience is valuable evidence about implementation, while leaving patient experience and frontline clinical use only partly addressed. A national record repository therefore needs to be evaluated through reliability, usability, and demonstrated care benefits as well as the information it stores. [s1]

content.heading: Remote services depend on institutions as well as connections
content.content:
Telemedicine uses communication technology to support care across distance. Iranian policymakers interviewed for research conducted in 2022 described obstacles involving policy, operating arrangements, telecommunications, public acceptance, electronic infrastructure, bureaucracy, law, and finance. They proposed stronger national commitment, a roadmap, better infrastructure, and preparation for adoption. Those proposals establish the researchers’ recommendations, rather than proof of completed reform. [s3]

The distinction between an available technology and a dependable service is especially important here. A consultation platform needs workable arrangements for professional responsibility, payment, privacy, and organizational cooperation. The study’s findings support examining these conditions together, rather than treating connectivity as the sole explanation for adoption. They do not establish the current legal position of every remote-care service or its coverage by insurance. [s3]

content.summary: This simplified diagram follows the information-transfer architecture described in the SEPAS evaluation. Its arrows represent record generation, transfer, and storage; they do not establish universal clinical access or complete coverage.

content.heading: Following the branches
content.content: The child pages separate records, hospital management, telemedicine, appointment booking, analytics, and monitoring so that their different purposes can be examined directly. The strongest inspected evidence here concerns electronic records and barriers to remote care. A fuller account still needs verified evidence about booking services, analytics deployments, and monitoring tools. Across the researched systems, the useful question is how information becomes reliable and usable in care, with benefits assessed in the setting where the technology operates. [s1][s2][s3]
